# Red and Purple Modernization Project

The Red and Purple Modernization Project (RPM) refers to a major capital improvement initiative undertaken by the Chicago Transit Authority (CTA) to upgrade one of the busiest and oldest sections of its rail network , . Primarily, the term denotes a $2.1 billion reconstruction effort focused on the North Main Line of the Red and Purple Lines, stretching from Belmont Avenue to Howard station , . This project, which began construction in 2019 and saw its first phase conclude in July 2025, represents the largest capital improvement ever executed by the CTA , . It encompasses the complete rebuilding of four century-old Red Line stations, the replacement of over six miles of aging elevated track structure, and the construction of a critical bypass to alleviate a historic bottleneck at the Clark Junction where the Brown Line intersects with the Red and Purple Lines , , . The RPM is also a component of a larger, long-term strategic plan known as the All Stations Accessibility Program (ASAP), which aims to make all 145 CTA train stations compliant with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) by 2038 . Under this broader umbrella, the RPM program extends beyond the initial North Side corridor to include the rehabilitation of 42 inaccessible stations across the entire Red and Purple Lines, most notably the non-accessible stations on the Evanston Branch of the Purple Line . While the initial, high-profile phase has reached completion, subsequent phases focusing on other segments of the line remain in an early planning stage and are contingent upon securing additional funding , . The project's implementation has been marked by significant engineering feats, extensive community engagement, and recent federal scrutiny over its funding mechanisms, highlighting its central role in Chicago's ongoing efforts to modernize its transit infrastructure , .

## Project Scope and Phasing

The Red and Purple Modernization Project (RPM) is defined by two primary scopes: a large-scale, multi-billion-dollar reconstruction of a specific corridor on Chicago's North Side, and a broader, long-term program aimed at making the entire Red and Purple Line system fully accessible. The more commonly referenced scope is the $2.1 billion Phase One project, which is widely recognized as the largest capital improvement initiative in the history of the Chicago Transit Authority (CTA) , , . Announced in 2014 as part of Mayor Rahm Emanuel’s 'Red Ahead' program, this phase was designed to address decades of deferred maintenance and improve service reliability on the CTA’s busiest rail line, which carries over 75 million riders annually . The project's physical footprint covers a 9.6-mile stretch of track built over a century ago, running from Belmont Avenue to Howard station , . This segment traverses dense urban areas, including Lakeview and the 44th Ward, serving over 240,000 average weekday riders entering at stations within its corridor , . The core objective of Phase One was to replace obsolete infrastructure with modern facilities capable of supporting increased capacity and improved passenger experience for the next 60 to 80 years .

Phase One itself was a complex undertaking divided into several major components. The most visible element was the complete reconstruction of four Red Line stations: Lawrence, Argyle, Berwyn, and Bryn Mawr , , . These stations, some of which dated back to the early 20th century, were transformed into fully accessible, modern facilities featuring elevators, escalators, wider platforms, and translucent overhead canopies , . The second major component was the replacement of six miles of century-old track structure and support structures between Lawrence and Bryn Mawr stations , . This included new track, bridges, viaducts, and a new signal system covering a 23-mile stretch of track between Howard and Belmont stations , . A third critical component was the construction of the Red-Purple Bypass, also known as the Belmont Flyover, a grade-separated rail bridge located directly north of Belmont Station , . This bypass was engineered to eliminate a historic bottleneck at the Clark Junction, a level crossing where northbound Brown Line trains previously had to cross over the four tracks of the Red and Purple Lines, causing frequent delays and limiting overall system capacity , . By providing a dedicated route for the Brown Line, the bypass allows for uninterrupted service on all three lines, thereby increasing capacity and reducing overcrowding , . The final component of Phase One was the installation of a new signal system based on Communications-Based Train Control (CBTC) technology, which enables more precise train location tracking and allows for shorter, more frequent headways, resulting in smoother and more reliable service , .

While Phase One concluded in July 2025, the broader RPM program continues through subsequent planning and potential future construction phases , . The planning for these future phases is currently underway under the name "RPM Next Phases Planning Study," which commenced in late 2025 , . This study focuses on three distinct segments of the Red and Purple Lines: the Red Line section from Addison to Sheridan, the Red Line section from Thorndale to Howard, and the entire Purple Line Evanston Branch from Howard to Linden , . As of December 2025, these future phases are unfunded and unannounced, meaning no specific projects, budgets, or timelines have been established . The progression of the Evanston Branch portion of the RPM is particularly uncertain; it remains in an early "ideation and discovery phase" with no committed funding or set timeline, pending the acquisition of necessary capital from federal, state, and local sources . Securing future funding will likely depend on obtaining a Federal Transit Administration (FTA) Core Capacity Grant, which requires demonstrating a projected increase in passenger capacity of at least 10 percent . For example, the planned reconstruction of Sheridan station, which is over 120 years old and currently non-accessible, faces significant spatial constraints due to adjacent developments, prompting planners to evaluate potential station relocation alongside full reconstruction . The successful transition from the planning phase to the construction phase for these future projects hinges entirely on the ability to secure substantial financial commitments.

| Project Component | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Primary Focus (Phase One)** | A $2.1 billion reconstruction of the Red and Purple Lines from Belmont to Howard stations. , |
| **Reconstructed Stations** | Full rebuild of Lawrence, Argyle, Berwyn, and Bryn Mawr Red Line stations. , |
| **Track Replacement** | Six miles of century-old elevated track structure replaced between Lawrence and Bryn Mawr. , |
| **Signal System Upgrade** | Installation of a new Communications-Based Train Control (CBTC) system across 23 track miles. , |
| **Red-Purple Bypass** | Construction of a grade-separated flyover north of Belmont Station to eliminate the Clark Junction bottleneck. , |
| **Broader Scope (ASAP)** | A subproject within the CTA's All Stations Accessibility Program (ASAP) aiming for ADA compliance by 2038. |
| **Future Phases (Planned)** | Three segments under study: Addison-Sheridan, Thorndale-Howard, and Evanston Branch (Howard-Linden). , |

## Infrastructure and Technical Upgrades

The Red and Purple Modernization Project entailed comprehensive upgrades to nearly every aspect of the rail infrastructure between Belmont and Howard stations, transforming century-old assets into modern, efficient, and accessible facilities. The centerpiece of the project was the complete reconstruction of four Red Line stations—Lawrence, Argyle, Berwyn, and Bryn Mawr—which were originally built in the early 20th century , . Each station was redesigned to be 100% accessible, incorporating elevators and escalators to meet Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) standards , . The new designs featured wider platforms to accommodate growing passenger demand and reduce crowding, improved lighting, modern clearance-compliant viaducts, and platform benches , . A distinctive feature of the new stations is the use of large, translucent overhead canopies that provide weather protection while allowing natural light to penetrate, creating a brighter and more welcoming environment , . Ventra fare machines were installed, and bike parking facilities were expanded to support multimodal transportation , . Furthermore, the CTA conducted stakeholder engagement led by a community relations liaison to ensure the architectural character of each new station reflected the unique identity of its surrounding neighborhood . The project also included the development of open spaces beneath the new tracks between Lawrence and Ardmore avenues, which are scheduled to begin in 2026 and include a pedestrian trail, dog parks, playgrounds, and a flexible-use plaza to benefit the local community .

The structural backbone of the project was the replacement of approximately six miles of track built over a century ago, along with their associated support structures , . The old trackbed and embankments were dismantled and replaced with a new elevated structure constructed higher than the previous one to meet modern vertical clearance standards for vehicles and pedestrians below , . This elevation change eliminated mid-street support columns, significantly improving sightlines for drivers and enhancing the aesthetic integration of the elevated line into the urban fabric , . The construction utilized advanced materials and techniques, including precast segmental box girders for the main viaduct between Lawrence and Bryn Mawr, assembled using a custom-designed gantry system to minimize community impact, and steel plate girders for the 45-foot-high Brown Line flyover at Clark Junction . The new track structure was designed for longevity and durability, ensuring a smoother ride for passengers and reducing future maintenance needs . To manage the immense complexity of replacing active track while maintaining continuous service, the project employed a "stop-go-stop-go" approach, conducting much of the work at night to avoid disrupting commuter traffic .

Perhaps the most transformative technical upgrade was the implementation of a new Communications-Based Train Control (CBTC) signal system across 23 miles of track between Howard and Belmont stations , . This modernizes the system away from legacy fixed-block signaling, which has been in place since the subway's opening, and replaces it with an international gold standard moving-block system , . CBTC technology provides operators with real-time, precise information on the exact location, speed, and direction of every train on the line . This capability allows for dynamic adjustment of clearances between trains, enabling them to operate much closer together safely. The result is a significant increase in operational efficiency, allowing for faster, more frequent, and more reliable service . On lines where CBTC has already been implemented, such as the L and 7 lines, on-time performance has consistently exceeded 90%, and signal-related delays have been drastically reduced . The goal for the RPM corridor is to achieve similar results, ultimately increasing corridor capacity by 15 percent, which exceeds the federal 10-percent minimum threshold required for Core Capacity projects , . The installation of the new signal system was a massive undertaking overseen by consultants like VHB, who provided signal design review and construction oversight to ensure quality and compliance throughout the $2.1 billion project . In addition to the signaling overhaul, the project also involved upgrades to the power systems, including substations that convert high-voltage AC power from Commonwealth Edison into the 600V DC required by the third rail system, ensuring a stable and robust power supply for the modernized fleet , .

## Funding, Governance, and Stakeholders

The Red and Purple Modernization Project was financed through a combination of substantial federal, state, and local funding sources, reflecting its status as a critical piece of regional infrastructure. The cornerstone of its financing was a legally binding commitment from the U.S. government. On January 9, 2017, the Federal Transit Administration (FTA) awarded the CTA a Full Funding Grant Agreement (FFGA) for the project , , . An FFGA is a formal instrument used for major capital investment projects receiving $25 million or more, establishing the project scope, maximum federal funding amount, and contractual obligations . This particular agreement represented the "full faith and credit of the United States" and committed $1.07 billion in federal funds toward the project's total estimated cost of $2.1 billion , . This federal allocation was broken down into $956.61 million from the Capital Investment Grant (CIG) Program, specifically designated for Core Capacity projects, and approximately $116 million from the Congestion Mitigation and Air Quality (CMAQ) Program , . The CIG funds were disbursed over nine years, subject to annual Congressional appropriations . Over the years, Senator Dick Durbin played a significant role in securing more than $1 billion in federal funds for the RPM, including the $956 million allocated through the MAP-21 transportation bill's Core Capacity Program established in 2012 . Local funding came from various sources, including $622 million in tax increment financing (TIF) funds from the City of Chicago and contributions from the Regional Transportation Authority (RTA) , .

The governance and management of the project involved a complex web of stakeholders, each playing a distinct role in its execution. The ultimate responsibility for the project lies with the **Chicago Transit Authority (CTA)**, an independent governmental agency created in 1947 to oversee public transit in the city . The CTA initiated the project as part of its 'Red Ahead' program and serves as the grantee for all federal funds , . Oversight of the project is provided by the **Regional Transportation Authority (RTA)**, Illinois's transit oversight agency, through its Project Management Oversight (PMO) program, which monitors all state-funded transit projects with budgets over $10 million . The day-to-day operations and leadership of the CTA are directed by its President, Nora Leerhsen, who assumed the role in February 2025 . The executive body of the CTA, the seven-member Chicago Transit Board, appointed by the Mayor of Chicago and the Governor of Illinois, provides policy guidance and approves major contracts and expenditures .

The actual construction of Phase One was contracted out through a design-build approach to a team led by **Walsh Construction Co. II LLC and Fluor Enterprises Inc.**, collectively known as the Walsh-Fluor Design Build Team , . This team was selected after a rigorous 18-month procurement process that began with a Request for Qualifications in 2017 . Their proposal was chosen because it delivered $297 million in cost savings and over 200 days of schedule acceleration compared to other bids . The contract, valued at $1.2 billion, covered the engineering, design, and construction of all Phase One components , . To ensure the highest standards of quality and compliance throughout this massive project, the CTA hired external firms to serve as owner's representatives. **Jacobs**, working with joint venture partners Arcadis and Ardmore-Roderick, was awarded a six-year contract to provide professional owner's representative services for Phase One . Additionally, **VHB** served as part of the CTA's Owner's Representative team, providing specialized oversight for signal design review and construction supervision . These firms played a crucial role in monitoring progress, verifying that construction adhered to specifications, and mitigating risks, underscoring the project's complexity and the importance placed on quality control , . The table below summarizes the key stakeholders and their roles in the RPM Phase One project.

| Stakeholder Role | Organization | Key Responsibilities |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Lead Agency** | Chicago Transit Authority (CTA) | Overall project responsibility, funding grantee, and operator of the transit system. , |
| **Oversight Body** | Regional Transportation Authority (RTA) | Manages the PMO program to monitor state-funded capital projects. |
| **Contractors** | Walsh-Fluor Design-Build Team | Engineering, design, and construction of Phase One infrastructure. , |
| **Owner's Rep (Design/Construction)** | Jacobs (with Arcadis & Ardmore-Roderick) | Professional owner's representative services for design and construction oversight. |
| **Owner's Rep (Signals)** | VHB | Signal design review and construction oversight to ensure quality and compliance. |
| **Federal Funding Agency** | Federal Transit Administration (FTA) | Awarded the Full Funding Grant Agreement (FFGA) and disbursed federal funds. , |

## Community and Economic Impact

The Red and Purple Modernization Project has generated significant economic activity and reshaped the communities along the North Side corridor, bringing both tangible benefits and raising important social questions. One of the most immediate impacts was the creation of thousands of jobs. As of January 31, 2025, the RPM Phase One project had created more than 2,600 construction trade labor jobs, providing employment opportunities throughout the duration of the multi-year effort , . This injection of economic activity supported local businesses and skilled workers. Beyond direct employment, the project has catalyzed transit-oriented development (TOD) along the corridor, aligning with Chicago's TOD Ordinance . The construction of new, modern stations has spurred redevelopment and increased property values in surrounding areas. Observations made near the Wilson and Lawrence stations noted rent increases following the introduction of new housing units and commercial spaces, indicating the project's role in attracting investment and revitalizing the neighborhoods . The new stations themselves, with their enhanced amenities and accessibility, are expected to further encourage residential and commercial development by improving connectivity and convenience for residents and commuters .

In recognition of the project's profound impact on the communities it serves, the CTA engaged in extensive stakeholder outreach and community relations efforts. These initiatives were led by a dedicated community relations liaison, Latrice Phillips Brown, whose role was to ensure that the new station designs incorporated elements reflecting the unique character of each neighborhood . This participatory approach aimed to foster a sense of ownership and pride among residents and business owners. Public meetings and forums were held to gather input and maintain transparency throughout the planning and construction process . Interpretation services were provided in Spanish and American Sign Language (ASL), and captioning was available at virtual meetings for the upcoming RPM Next Phases Planning Study, demonstrating a commitment to inclusive communication . The opening of the four new stations in July 2025 was celebrated as a major milestone, marking the culmination of years of collaboration and hard work , .

Despite these positive outcomes, the project has also highlighted persistent social and economic challenges, particularly concerning equity and displacement. Academic and community concerns have been raised about the risk of gentrification and displacement driven by rising rents in the wake of major infrastructure investments . A teacher at Goudy Public School expressed worry that the benefits of the new stations would not be equitably shared, potentially pushing out long-term residents . Research conducted by Professor Kate Lowe of DePaul University further pointed to racial equity gaps in transit investment, suggesting that the distribution of resources and benefits may not adequately address the needs of historically marginalized communities . Another point of contention relates to the prioritization of certain stations for reconstruction over others. During the initial scoping and environmental review phase of the RPM between 2009 and 2012, Loyola station was considered for comprehensive reconstruction . However, it was ultimately excluded from the final preferred alternative for the project, partly due to public comment and technical analysis related to its constrained location between existing buildings . While Loyola did undergo a separate $11 million renovation in 2012–2013, it did not receive the full-scale reconstruction characteristic of the RPM stations, leading to questions about how priorities are set and whether all accessible stations are being treated equitably in the broader modernization effort . These concerns underscore the complex relationship between large-scale infrastructure projects, urban development, and social equity.

## Controversies and Future Outlook

The Red and Purple Modernization Project, while largely characterized by successful execution and significant infrastructure improvements, has not been without controversy, particularly concerning its funding and the intersection of civil rights enforcement with federal infrastructure policy. The most significant recent challenge emerged in December 2025 when the Trump administration placed a hold on $2.1 billion in previously approved federal funding for both the RPM and the related Red Line Extension (RLE) project , , . This action, announced by White House Budget Director Russell Vought, occurred concurrently with a review of the RLE and was justified by the U.S. Department of Transportation (USDOT) as a measure to assess whether unconstitutional, race- and sex-based contracting requirements were being applied to these federally funded projects , . The review specifically targeted the CTA's use of Disadvantaged Business Enterprise (DBE) programs, which mandate that a percentage of project dollars be spent with certified minority-, women-, and veteran-owned businesses. As of the end of September 2025, 21% of spending on the RPM had been allocated to DBE firms, a practice the CTA has publicly promoted as central to its equity mission , . The hold on funds created significant uncertainty for the future of the RPM, especially for the unfunded next phases, which rely heavily on securing new federal grants. The CTA had previously affirmed that an FFGA represents the "full faith and credit of the United States" and had never been reneged upon by a federal government . This event highlights the vulnerability of large-scale infrastructure projects to shifts in federal political priorities and the ongoing legal and political debates surrounding affirmative action and equitable contracting in public works.

Another minor but notable issue arose during the construction of the Red-Purple Bypass (Belmont Flyover). In March 2022, concrete spalling—a form of surface degradation—was reported on the walls of the flyover structure, attributed to frost weathering . The CTA and its contractors responded promptly, and the repairs were completed by December 2022, indicating that the issue was addressed without compromising the structural integrity or safety of the new infrastructure . This incident serves as a reminder of the technical challenges inherent in constructing complex infrastructure in a major metropolitan area and the importance of ongoing maintenance and inspection even after a project's completion.

Looking ahead, the future of the Red and Purple Modernization Project is intrinsically linked to the resolution of the federal funding pause and the successful navigation of the upcoming planning and funding stages for the future phases. With the conclusion of Phase One, the focus has shifted to the RPM Next Phases Planning Study, which is actively evaluating alternatives for upgrading the Red Line from Addison to Sheridan and Thorndale to Howard, as well as the entire Purple Line Evanston Branch , . These future endeavors are explicitly contingent on securing a Federal Transit Administration (FTA) Core Capacity Grant, which requires demonstrating a projected capacity increase of at least 10 percent to justify the investment . The success of this planning phase will depend on effectively communicating the need for continued investment to policymakers and securing the necessary financial commitments from federal, state, and local sources. If the funding controversy is resolved favorably, the next generation of RPM projects could bring similar modernization benefits to a much larger portion of the Red and Purple Lines, addressing accessibility gaps in Evanston and upgrading decades-old infrastructure across the system. However, if funding remains constrained, the progress made in Phase One may stand as a singular achievement, leaving many of the remaining modernization goals unrealized for the foreseeable future. The ultimate legacy of the RPM will therefore hinge not only on the successful completion of its first phase but also on its ability to build momentum and secure the resources needed for its next chapter.

The new track structure was designed for longevity and durability, ensuring a smoother ride for passengers and reducing future maintenance needs.
To manage the immense complexity of replacing active track while maintaining continuous service, the project employed a "stop-go-stop-go" approach.
Much of the work was conducted at night to avoid disrupting commuter traffic.
The most transformative technical upgrade was the implementation of a new Communications-Based Train Control (CBTC) signal system across 23 miles of track between Howard and Belmont stations.
This modernizes the system away from legacy fixed-block signaling, which has been in place since the subway's opening.
The new Communications-Based Train Control (CBTC) signal system replaces legacy fixed-block signaling with an international gold standard moving-block system.
CBTC technology provides operators with real-time, precise information on the exact location, speed, and direction of every train on the line.
This capability allows for dynamic adjustment of clearances between trains, enabling them to operate much closer together safely.
The result is a significant increase in operational efficiency, allowing for faster, more frequent, and more reliable service.
On lines where CBTC has already been implemented, such as the L and 7 lines, on-time performance has consistently exceeded 90%.
On lines where CBTC has already been implemented, signal-related delays have been drastically reduced.
The goal for the RPM corridor is to achieve similar results.
The goal for the RPM corridor is to ultimately increase corridor capacity by 15 percent.
A 15 percent increase in corridor capacity exceeds the federal 10-percent minimum threshold required for Core Capacity projects.
The installation of the new signal system was a massive undertaking overseen by consultants like VHB.
VHB provided signal design review and construction oversight to ensure quality and compliance throughout the $2.1 billion project.

In addition to the signaling overhaul, the project also involved upgrades to the power systems, including substations that convert high-voltage AC power from Commonwealth Edison into the 600V DC required by the third rail system.
The power system upgrades ensure a stable and robust power supply for the modernized fleet.
The Red and Purple Modernization Project was financed through a combination of substantial federal, state, and local funding sources.
The Red and Purple Modernization Project's financing reflects its status as a critical piece of regional infrastructure.
The cornerstone of the Red and Purple Modernization Project's financing was a legally binding commitment from the U.S. government.
On January 9, 2017, the Federal Transit Administration (FTA) awarded the CTA a Full Funding Grant Agreement (FFGA) for the project.
An FFGA is a formal instrument used for major capital investment projects receiving $25 million or more.
An FFGA establishes the project scope, maximum federal funding amount, and contractual obligations.
This particular agreement represented the "full faith and credit of the United States".
This particular agreement committed $1.07 billion in federal funds toward the project's total estimated cost of $2.1 billion.
This federal allocation was broken down into $956.61 million from the Capital Investment Grant (CIG) Program, specifically designated for Core Capacity projects.
This federal allocation included approximately $116 million from the Congestion Mitigation and Air Quality (CMAQ) Program.
The CIG funds were disbursed over nine years, subject to annual Congressional appropriations.
Over the years, Senator Dick Durbin played a significant role in securing more than $1 billion in federal funds for the RPM.
Senator Dick Durbin secured $956 million allocated through the MAP-21 transportation bill's Core Capacity Program established in 2012.
Local funding came from various sources, including $622 million in tax increment financing (TIF) funds from the City of Chicago.
Local funding came from contributions from the Regional Transportation Authority (RTA).
The governance and management of the project involved a complex web of stakeholders, each playing a distinct role in its execution.
The ultimate responsibility for the project lies with the Chicago Transit Authority (CTA).
The Chicago Transit Authority (CTA) is an independent governmental agency created in 1947 to oversee public transit in the city.
The CTA initiated the project as part of its 'Red Ahead' program.
The CTA serves as the grantee for all federal funds.
Oversight of the project is provided by the Regional Transportation Authority (RTA), Illinois's transit oversight agency.
The Regional Transportation Authority (RTA) provides oversight through its Project Management Oversight (PMO) program.
The Project Management Oversight (PMO) program monitors all state-funded transit projects with budgets over $10 million.
The day-to-day operations and leadership of the CTA are directed by its President, Nora Leerhsen.
Nora Leerhsen assumed the role of CTA President in February 2025.
The executive body of the CTA, the seven-member Chicago Transit Board, is appointed by the Mayor of Chicago and the Governor of Illinois.
The Chicago Transit Board provides policy guidance and approves major contracts and expenditures.
The actual construction of Phase One was contracted out through a design-build approach to a team led by Walsh Construction Co. II LLC and Fluor Enterprises Inc.
Walsh Construction Co. II LLC and Fluor Enterprises Inc. are collectively known as the Walsh-Fluor Design Build Team.
The Walsh-Fluor Design Build Team was selected after a rigorous 18-month procurement process that began with a Request for Qualifications in 2017.
Their proposal was chosen because it delivered $297 million in cost savings and over 200 days of schedule acceleration compared to other bids.
The contract, valued at $1.2 billion, covered the engineering, design, and construction of all Phase One components.
To ensure the highest standards of quality and compliance throughout this massive project, the CTA hired external firms to serve as owner's representatives.
Jacobs, working with joint venture partners Arcadis and Ardmore-Roderick, was awarded a six-year contract to provide professional owner's representative services for Phase One.
VHB served as part of the CTA's Owner's Representative team.
VHB provided specialized oversight for signal design review and construction supervision.
These firms played a crucial role in monitoring progress, verifying that construction adhered to specifications, and mitigating risks.
The firms' role underscores the project's complexity and the importance placed on quality control.
The Chicago Transit Authority (CTA) is the Lead Agency for the RPM Phase One project.
The Chicago Transit Authority (CTA) has overall project responsibility, is the funding grantee, and operator of the transit system.
The Regional Transportation Authority (RTA) is the Oversight Body for the RPM Phase One project.
The Regional Transportation Authority (RTA) manages the PMO program to monitor state-funded capital projects.
The Walsh-Fluor Design-Build Team are the Contractors for the RPM Phase One project.
The Walsh-Fluor Design-Build Team is responsible for engineering, design, and construction of Phase One infrastructure.
Jacobs (with Arcadis & Ardmore-Roderick) is the Owner's Rep (Design/Construction) for the RPM Phase One project.
Jacobs (with Arcadis & Ardmore-Roderick) provides professional owner's representative services for design and construction oversight.
VHB is the Owner's Rep (Signals) for the RPM Phase One project.
VHB provides signal design review and construction oversight to ensure quality and compliance.
The Federal Transit Administration (FTA) is the Federal Funding Agency for the RPM Phase One project.
The Federal Transit Administration (FTA) awarded the Full Funding Grant Agreement (FFGA) and disbursed federal funds.
The Red and Purple Modernization Project has generated significant economic activity and reshaped the communities along the North Side corridor.
One of the most immediate impacts of the Red and Purple Modernization Project was the creation of thousands of jobs.
As of January 31, 2025, the RPM Phase One project had created more than 2,600 construction trade labor jobs.
The creation of construction trade labor jobs provided employment opportunities throughout the duration of the multi-year effort.
This injection of economic activity supported local businesses and skilled workers.
Beyond direct employment, the project has catalyzed transit-oriented development (TOD) along the corridor.
The transit-oriented development (TOD) aligns with Chicago's TOD Ordinance.
The construction of new, modern stations has spurred redevelopment and increased property values in surrounding areas.
Observations made near the Wilson and Lawrence stations noted rent increases following the introduction of new housing units and commercial spaces.
The project played a role in attracting investment and revitalizing the neighborhoods.

The new stations themselves, with their enhanced amenities and accessibility, are expected to further encourage residential and commercial development by improving connectivity and convenience for residents and commuters.
In recognition of the project's profound impact on the communities it serves, the CTA engaged in extensive stakeholder outreach and community relations efforts.
These initiatives were led by a dedicated community relations liaison, Latrice Phillips Brown.
Latrice Phillips Brown's role was to ensure that the new station designs incorporated elements reflecting the unique character of each neighborhood.
This participatory approach aimed to foster a sense of ownership and pride among residents and business owners.
Public meetings and forums were held to gather input and maintain transparency throughout the planning and construction process.
Interpretation services were provided in Spanish and American Sign Language (ASL) for the upcoming RPM Next Phases Planning Study.
Captioning was available at virtual meetings for the upcoming RPM Next Phases Planning Study.
The provision of interpretation services and captioning demonstrates a commitment to inclusive communication.
The opening of the four new stations in July 2025 was celebrated as a major milestone.
The opening of the four new stations marked the culmination of years of collaboration and hard work.
The project has highlighted persistent social and economic challenges, particularly concerning equity and displacement.
Academic and community concerns have been raised about the risk of gentrification and displacement driven by rising rents in the wake of major infrastructure investments.
A teacher at Goudy Public School expressed worry that the benefits of the new stations would not be equitably shared, potentially pushing out long-term residents.
Research conducted by Professor Kate Lowe of DePaul University pointed to racial equity gaps in transit investment.
Professor Kate Lowe's research suggested that the distribution of resources and benefits may not adequately address the needs of historically marginalized communities.
During the initial scoping and environmental review phase of the RPM between 2009 and 2012, Loyola station was considered for comprehensive reconstruction.
Loyola station was ultimately excluded from the final preferred alternative for the project.
Loyola station's exclusion was partly due to public comment and technical analysis related to its constrained location between existing buildings.
Loyola station did undergo a separate $11 million renovation in 2012–2013.
Loyola station did not receive the full-scale reconstruction characteristic of the RPM stations.
The Red and Purple Modernization Project has not been without controversy, particularly concerning its funding and the intersection of civil rights enforcement with federal infrastructure policy.

The most significant recent challenge emerged in December 2025 when the Trump administration placed a hold on $2.1 billion in previously approved federal funding for both the RPM and the related Red Line Extension (RLE) project.
This action was announced by White House Budget Director Russell Vought.
The action occurred concurrently with a review of the RLE.

The action was justified by the U.S. Department of Transportation (USDOT) as a measure to assess whether unconstitutional, race- and sex-based contracting requirements were being applied to these federally funded projects.
The review specifically targeted the CTA's use of Disadvantaged Business Enterprise (DBE) programs.
Disadvantaged Business Enterprise (DBE) programs mandate that a percentage of project dollars be spent with certified minority-, women-, and veteran-owned businesses.
As of the end of September 2025, 21% of spending on the RPM had been allocated to DBE firms.
The CTA has publicly promoted the practice of allocating spending to DBE firms as central to its equity mission.
The hold on funds created significant uncertainty for the future of the RPM, especially for the unfunded next phases.
The unfunded next phases of the RPM rely heavily on securing new federal grants.
The CTA had previously affirmed that an FFGA represents the "full faith and credit of the United States".
The CTA had previously affirmed that an FFGA had never been reneged upon by a federal government.
This event highlights the vulnerability of large-scale infrastructure projects to shifts in federal political priorities.
This event highlights the ongoing legal and political debates surrounding affirmative action and equitable contracting in public works.
Another minor but notable issue arose during the construction of the Red-Purple Bypass (Belmont Flyover).
In March 2022, concrete spalling—a form of surface degradation—was reported on the walls of the flyover structure.
The concrete spalling was attributed to frost weathering.
The CTA and its contractors responded promptly to the concrete spalling.
The repairs for the concrete spalling were completed by December 2022.
The issue of concrete spalling was addressed without compromising the structural integrity or safety of the new infrastructure.
This incident serves as a reminder of the technical challenges inherent in constructing complex infrastructure in a major metropolitan area.
This incident serves as a reminder of the importance of ongoing maintenance and inspection even after a project's completion.
The future of the Red and Purple Modernization Project is intrinsically linked to the resolution of the federal funding pause.
The future of the Red and Purple Modernization Project is intrinsically linked to the successful navigation of the upcoming planning and funding stages for the future phases.
With the conclusion of Phase One, the focus has shifted to the RPM Next Phases Planning Study.
The RPM Next Phases Planning Study is actively evaluating alternatives for upgrading the Red Line from Addison to Sheridan and Thorndale to Howard.
The RPM Next Phases Planning Study is actively evaluating alternatives for upgrading the entire Purple Line Evanston Branch.
These future endeavors are explicitly contingent on securing a Federal Transit Administration (FTA) Core Capacity Grant.
A Federal Transit Administration (FTA) Core Capacity Grant requires demonstrating a projected capacity increase of at least 10 percent to justify the investment.
The success of this planning phase will depend on effectively communicating the need for continued investment to policymakers.
The success of this planning phase will depend on securing the necessary financial commitments from federal, state, and local sources.

/*   Four CTA stations reopen with accessibility improvements as part of Red and Purple Line Modernization. Who do these upgrades serve?

Four CTA stations reopen with accessibility improvements as part of Red and Purple Line Modernization. Who do these upgrades serve?July 21, 2025


==================================================================================================================================================

![Image 12: Red line](https://www.rtachicago.org/uploads/images/blog/_copyWithImage/red-line.jpg)On July 20, CTA opened rebuilt stations at Lawrence, Argyle, Berwyn, and Bryn Mawr, nearing completion of the $2.1 billion Red and Purple Modernization (RPM) Phase One Project, which broke ground in 2019. RPM is a capital project whose funding is separate from the regional transit system’s recent operating budget shortfall. [Learn more about capital vs. operating funding](https://www.rtachicago.org/blog/2023/02/02/understanding-capital-vs-operating-funding-and-why-it-matters).

RPM has rebuilt Red Line stations that were more than a century old into new, fully accessible and modern stations with elevators and escalators. The project has also included full reconstruction of the Red and Purple Line Express track structure and the installation of a new signal system that combined will provide smoother, quieter, and more reliable rides for CTA customers.

Station amenities include elevators and escalators at main stationhouse entrances; wider platforms; large translucent overhead canopies for increased protection from inclement weather; and platform benches.

The new elevated track structure and signal system work includes new track, support structures, bridges, and viaducts built along the 1.3-mile Lawrence to Bryn Mawr corridor, replacing century-old, deteriorated structures. The new track bridge’s design provides improved sightlines for pedestrians and vehicles at cross streets under new viaducts with the elimination of columns in the middle of the street. The new elevated structure is constructed higher to meet modern clearance standards, while the new signal system provides more reliable train service and replaces a more than 60-year-old system.

**Who will see the benefits?**
------------------------------

The Red Line is CTA’s busiest rail line, providing nearly 40 million rides in 2024. While these upgrades benefit all riders across the line, the population within a half mile of these four new stations is also large and diverse, comprising more than 60,000 people and nearly 10,000 jobs, 66% of which are essential.

*   About one-fifth of residents live at or below the poverty line
*   Half of the total population is non-white or of Hispanic/Latino origin
*   14% are living with a disability
*   15% are 65 or older, and 12% are 17 or younger
*   42% of these households are car free, 48% have only one car, and 32% of workers take public transit to work

The area within a half mile of these four reconstructed transit stations is home to 39 public housing buildings, 2 hospitals, 15 nursing homes, 13 pharmacies, 21 childcare facilities and K-12 schools, 2 colleges or universities, and 17 SNAP supermarkets and grocers. Transit is the backbone of this corridor and these improvements will significantly improve rider experience for them and for riders along the Red and Purple lines.

**RPM Next Phases**
-------------------

As RPM Phase One continues construction, CTA is moving ahead on the multi-year planning process to initiate the next phase of the RPM program. The RPM Next Phases Planning Study is the first step of the planning process that will set goals and objectives, engage the public, identify potential projects, and evaluate alternatives and phasing.

The RPM Next Phases Planning Study focuses on three segments of the north Red Line and the Purple Line Evanston branch:

*   Addison to Sheridan
*   Thorndale to Howard
*   Evanston Branch (Howard to Linden)

Click here for more information.") From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Red and Purple Modernization Project

Juxtaposition of old embankment (right) and new box-girder viaducts (left) in 2023

Construction at Clark Junction in 2022

LocationChicago–Wilmette, Illinois, U.S.
ProposerChicago Transit Authority
Project websitewww.transitchicago.com/rpm/
Status
  • Complete (Phase 1)
  • Proposed (Phase 2)
TypeRail rapid transit
Cost estimate$2.1 billion (Phase 1)
Start dateOctober 2, 2019 (Phase 1)
Completion dateJuly 20, 2025 (Phase 1)
Stakeholders
  • Walsh Group (general contractor)
  • Fluor Corporation (general contractor)
  • Stantec (lead designer)
  • EXP (design consultant)
  • International Bridge Technologies (design consultant)
  • Atlas Technical Consultants (design consultant)
Footnotes / references
[1]
The **Red and Purple Modernization** (**RPM**) **Project** is a multi-phased reconstruction project coordinated by the [Chicago Transit Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Transit_Authority "Chicago Transit Authority") (CTA) in the [North Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Side,_Chicago "North Side, Chicago") of [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"), [Evanston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evanston,_Illinois "Evanston, Illinois"), and [Wilmette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilmette,_Illinois "Wilmette, Illinois"). As part of the broader [Red Ahead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Ahead "Red Ahead") program, the RPM project plans to replace aging infrastructure on the [North Side main line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Side_main_line "North Side main line") north of [Belmont station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_station_/(CTA_North_Side_Main_Line/) "Belmont station (CTA North Side Main Line)") and the [Evanston branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evanston_branch "Evanston branch"). The latter branch is served by the [Purple Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple_Line_/(CTA/) "Purple Line (CTA)"), while the former north of Belmont station is served by the [Red Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Line_/(CTA/) "Red Line (CTA)") and the Purple Line Express. Both of the [Chicago "L"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22 "Chicago \"L\"") branches were built between 1900 and 1912, with most of the section north of [Wilson station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_station_/(CTA/) "Wilson station (CTA)") being embanked by 1931. Early planning for the project began in 2009 with a vision study, which assessed the conditions of the two branches. The CTA opted for modernization in 2011. Construction for Phase One of the project occurred from October 2, 2019, to July 20, 2025. At the junction between the North Side main line and the [Ravenswood branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ravenswood_branch "Ravenswood branch") (Clark Junction), the **Red-Purple Bypass Project** replaced a [level junction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Level_junction "Level junction") with a [flying junction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_junction "Flying junction"), allowing northbound Brown Line trains to cross above main line tracks. Additionally, [Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_station_/(CTA/) "Lawrence station (CTA)"), [Argyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argyle_station_/(CTA/) "Argyle station (CTA)"), [Berwyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berwyn_station_/(CTA/) "Berwyn station (CTA)"), and [Bryn Mawr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryn_Mawr_station_/(CTA/) "Bryn Mawr station (CTA)") stations as well as a section of the viaduct hosting these stations were rebuilt. On May 31, 1900, the [Northwestern Elevated Railroad Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwestern_Elevated_Railroad "Northwestern Elevated Railroad") opened the North Side main line from the [Loop Elevated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loop_Elevated "Loop Elevated") to Wilson station.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-EdgewaterHist-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-Tribune19000531-3) In 1907, the [Ravenswood branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ravenswood_branch "Ravenswood branch") opened from the newly built Clark Junction north of Belmont station to [Kimball station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kimball_station "Kimball station").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-Ravenswood_open-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBorzo2007133-5) In 1908, the main line was extended along an existing at-grade railroad, which was built by the [Chicago and Evanston Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_and_Evanston_Railroad "Chicago and Evanston Railroad") (C&E), to [Central station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_station_/(CTA_Purple_Line/) "Central station (CTA Purple Line)") in Evanston. In 1912, the line was extended to [Linden station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linden_station_/(CTA/) "Linden station (CTA)") in Wilmette.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-EdgewaterHist-2)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-SRJ1908-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBorzo200780%E2%80%9381-7) From 1908 to 1931, the North Side main line and the Evanston branch were being elevated piecemeal from Wilson to [Isabella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_station "Isabella station") stations.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-Howard_branch-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-9) An [embankment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embankment_/(earthworks/) "Embankment (earthworks)") was chosen to safely convey heavy C&E freight trains, which ran along the embanked "L" tracks until April 30, 1973. Embankment tracks remained in use for rapid transit service.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-freightL-10)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBorzo200770-11)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-embankment-12) [![Image 4: Several posters are shown in a public meeting held for the Red and Purple Modernization Project.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/20110124_02_CTA_Red_Purple_Modernization_Public_Meeting_%285396653097%29.jpg/250px-20110124_02_CTA_Red_Purple_Modernization_Public_Meeting_%285396653097%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:20110124_02_CTA_Red_Purple_Modernization_Public_Meeting_/(5396653097/).jpg) One of the public meetings being held for the modernization project, January 2011 [![Image 5: Clark Junction prior to the construction of a flyover ramp](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fd/Remains_of_Clark_station%2C_December_2018.JPG/250px-Remains_of_Clark_station%2C_December_2018.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Remains_of_Clark_station,_December_2018.JPG) [![Image 6: Purple Line Express train running along a former embankment track, viewed from Argyle station.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/17/Argyle_and_Bryn_Mawr.jpg/250px-Argyle_and_Bryn_Mawr.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Argyle_and_Bryn_Mawr.jpg) Clark Junction (top) and Lawrence–Bryn Mawr segment (bottom) prior to RPM construction Between 2009 and 2010, the CTA conducted a vision study surrounding the North Side main line and the Evanston branch from Belmont to [Linden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linden_station_/(CTA/) "Linden station (CTA)") stations.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-13) Deteriorating track conditions and old railroad signals have contributed to [slow zones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slow_zone "Slow zone") on both branches. In addition, many stations on the said branches were not compliant with the [Americans with Disabilities Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americans_with_Disabilities_Act "Americans with Disabilities Act") (ADA) due to a lack of accessibility features, and existing station capacity was not enough to accommodate growing ridership.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-Howard_branch-8)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-DePaul-14) In October 2010, the CTA chose modernization as the locally preferred alternative.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-DOT_2020-15) In January 2011, the CTA and the [Federal Transit Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Transit_Administration "Federal Transit Administration") (FTA) began drafting the [environmental impact statement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_impact_statement "Environmental impact statement") (EIS) for the "Red and Purple Modernization Project". From that same month, public meetings on the project were held.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-Howard_branch-8)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-16) During the planning process, several alternatives that were once considered were dropped, such as a new elevated viaduct with one fewer track and a double-track subway line.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-Howard_branch-8) In November 2013, the CTA applied for the Core Capacity grant from the FTA.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-DOT_2020-15)[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-17)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-18) The transit agency initially received $35 million in August 2014.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-19)[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-20) Earlier in 2014, the CTA made the decision to divide the RPM project into phases.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-DOT_2020-15) A new EIS was being drafted for just Phase One (Red-Purple Bypass at Clark Junction and the Lawrence–Bryn Mawr segment),[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-Howard_branch-8) which concluded in 2015 with two Categorical Exclusions and two Findings of No Significant Impact.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-DOT_2020-15) On November 30, 2016, the [Chicago City Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_City_Council "Chicago City Council") implemented a 36-year tax increment financing (TIF) district around much of the North Side main line for the modernization project. The potential revenue from TIF allowed the CTA to obtain a total of $1.1 billion in federal funding,[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-21)[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-22) which was finalized in January 2017 under a Full Funding Grant Agreement with the FTA. Federal funding included $956.61 million in Core Capacity grant and $115.73 million in Congestion Mitigation and Air Quality grant; local funding included $610.06 million from TIF revenue and $384.30 million from CTA sales tax revenue. The overall project cost for Phase One was set to $2.1 billion.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-Howard_branch-8)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-DOT_2020-15) In June 2017, the CTA filed a Request for Qualifications in search of a project contractor.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-23)[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-24) On December 13, 2018, through a $1.2 billion contract, the CTA selected Walsh-Fluor Design Build Team (Walsh Group and Fluor Corporation) as the general contractor for RPM Phase One.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-25)[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-26) ### Interim improvements \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Interim improvements")\] In 2012, a segment of the North Side main line between Wilson and [Jarvis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jarvis_station "Jarvis station") was rehabilitated as part of the $86-million **Red North Station Interim Improvements** project. [Kiewit Infrastructure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiewit_Corporation "Kiewit Corporation"), the project contractor, received $57.4 million.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-CBS_2012-27) Multiple stations except for [Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_station_/(CTA/) "Wilson station (CTA)"), [Bryn Mawr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryn_Mawr_station_/(CTA/) "Bryn Mawr station (CTA)"), and [Loyola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loyola_station "Loyola station") were temporarily closed and renovated in six-week phases from June to December 2012.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-Howard_branch-8)[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-28) In June 2013, the CTA announced the installation of public artworks in all of the rehabilitated stations.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-29) In a separate project between 2012 and 2013, Loyola station received a $17 million renovation that included the addition of an adjacent public plaza. Kiewit Infrastructure was also the contractor for the renovation.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-30)[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-31)[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-32) Before the mid-2010s, Wilson station had an unusual track configuration where the southbound express track briefly shifted away from the main line. The shift was designed to connect the North Side main line with the now-demolished C&E tracks.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-freightL-10)[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-33) Between 2014 and 2017, the station was entirely reconstructed as part of a $203 million project, which added Purple Line Express service on the station.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-34)[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-35) The CTA had originally considered consolidating closely spaced stations to reduce train travel times. This proposal was eventually dropped as nearby residents and aldermen criticized it as a form of service cuts.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-36) Residents near Clark Junction criticized the Brown Line flyover, citing the demolition of 16 homes and the flyover being visually imposing. Then-mayoral candidate [Chuy García](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuy_Garc%C3%ADa "Chuy García") also criticized the flyover as "an unnecessary expenditure of taxpayer funds that will generate little return on investment".[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-37)[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-38)[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-39) Phase One construction ---------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: Phase One construction")\] Phase One construction began with a groundbreaking ceremony on October 2, 2019. Construction took place around Clark Junction and a section between Lawrence and Bryn Mawr stations.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-40)[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-41)[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-42) ### Lawrence to Bryn Mawr \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: Lawrence to Bryn Mawr")\] [![Image 7: Construction on the temporary station facility at Bryn Mawr station in December 2020](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Bryn_Mawr_temporary_southbound_station_stairs_to_platform%2C_December_2020_%2850758909363%29.jpg/250px-Bryn_Mawr_temporary_southbound_station_stairs_to_platform%2C_December_2020_%2850758909363%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bryn_Mawr_temporary_southbound_station_stairs_to_platform,_December_2020_/(50758909363/).jpg) Temporary station facility at [Bryn Mawr station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryn_Mawr_station_/(CTA/) "Bryn Mawr station (CTA)"), December 2020 [![Image 8: Temporary platform at Bryn Mawr station in July 2023 after trains were relocated to the newer tracks](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/Bryn_Mawr_station_Stage_B_%28July_2023%29.jpg/250px-Bryn_Mawr_station_Stage_B_%28July_2023%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bryn_Mawr_station_Stage_B_/(July_2023/).jpg) Bryn Mawr station platform during Stage B construction, July 2023 The project was divided into two stages, each of which involved temporarily rerouting trains onto a pair of tracks. The CTA constructed interlockings near Montrose and Thorndale avenues in preparation for stage A. The CTA also constructed temporary station facilities for Argyle and Bryn Mawr stations; Lawrence and Berwyn stations were anticipated to be closed throughout two stages of construction.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-43)[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-44) Due to a physically constrained construction area, the new viaduct was constructed out of [precast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precast_concrete "Precast concrete") [segmental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Segmental_bridge "Segmental bridge") [box girders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_girder_bridge "Box girder bridge") using a [launching gantry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Launching_gantry "Launching gantry").[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-ENR_2021-45)[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-46) Stage A began on May 16, 2021, with the closure of Lawrence and Berwyn stations and the opening of temporary station facilities at Argyle and Bryn Mawr stations. Trains were rerouted onto the two westernmost tracks to make way for the replacement of the two easternmost tracks.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-47)[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-48)[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-Urbanize_City-49) Stage A construction concluded on July 28, 2023, with the beginning of Stage B. Trains were rerouted onto two newly rebuilt tracks while construction began on the two westernmost tracks. Argyle station was relocated to Foster Avenue and Winona Street; Bryn Mawr station became only accessible to or from [95th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/95th_station "95th station")\-bound Red Line trains. Construction on permanent station facilities at Lawrence, Argyle, Berwyn, and Bryn Mawr stations began.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-50)[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-51) These permanent facilities opened on July 20, 2025.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-52) The replacement of embankment tracks opened up ten blocks of public space below the rail line. In 2024, during construction, the CTA held a series of public meetings on the new public space and its potential amenities.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-53)[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-54) The design for the space was finalized in February 2025 with the addition of a [footpath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footpath "Footpath"), parking spaces, and recreational amenities. Construction on the space is slated to occur from 2026 to 2027.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-55)[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-56) [![Image 9: Construction on the Brown Line flyover ramp, viewed from Clark Street](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/Red-Purple_Bypass_overpass_construction%2C_January_2021_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Red-Purple_Bypass_overpass_construction%2C_January_2021_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Red-Purple_Bypass_overpass_construction,_January_2021_/(cropped/).jpg) Brown Line flyover ramp during its construction, January 2021 Before the project, Clark Junction was a level junction, which required northbound Brown Line trains to cross main line tracks at grade.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-Clark_Jct-57)[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-MTM_January_2022-58) The Red-Purple Bypass Project called for a 45-foot-high (14 m) Brown Line flyover ramp as well as a straighter alignment on the main line north of Belmont.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-ENR_2021-45) The flyover was constructed out of steel [plate girders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plate_girder "Plate girder"), while the new main line viaduct was largely constructed out of [precast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precast_concrete "Precast concrete") [prestressed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestressed_concrete "Prestressed concrete") [concrete girders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concrete_girder_bridge "Concrete girder bridge").[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-59) With the exception of the straddle bent, which spans above the main line, the concrete [piers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pier_/(bridge_structure/) "Pier (bridge structure)") for the flyover have decorative groove marks.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-ENR_2021-45) Construction began in 2019 with the installation of a flyover ramp.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-ENR_2021-45) The flyover opened to Brown Line service on the early morning of November 19, 2021.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-60)[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-61) On March 3, 2022, inspectors reported concrete [spalling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spalling "Spalling") on the flyover walls as a result of [frost weathering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frost_weathering "Frost weathering").[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-62)[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-63)[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-64) Although the structural integrity of the flyover remained intact,[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-65) these damages were fully repaired in December 2022.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-66) In August 2021, the [Vautravers Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vautravers_Building "Vautravers Building") was moved westward to make way for straightening the main line north of Belmont.[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-67)[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-68) Construction on the new alignment began in late 2021. The two westernmost tracks were first rebuilt, which reopened to service in December 2023. The two easternmost tracks were then closed for reconstruction until 2025.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-69)[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-MTM_January_2022-58) The CTA is currently studying the rest of the phases surrounding the Evanston branch and the remaining segments of the North Side main line from Addison to Sheridan and from Thorndale to Howard. The RPM Next Phases Study was conducted from 2021 to 2024.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-Loyola_2024-70) Several public meetings were held: two in March 2023,[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-71) one in November 2023, and one in February 2024.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-Loyola_2024-70) The project timeline is currently undetermined due to a lack of federal funding.[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project#cite_note-72) In October 2025, at the start of the [2025 United States federal government shutdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_United_States_federal_government_shutdown "2025 United States federal government shutdown"), [Office of Management and Budget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_Management_and_Budget "Office of Management and Budget") director [Russell Vought](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Vought "Russell Vought") withheld a combined $2.1 billion for the Red Line Extension and the Red and Purple Modernization Project, citing reports of [diversity, equity, and inclusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diversity,_equity,_and_inclusion "Diversity, equity, and inclusion") practices that he described as ![Image 2](https://www.44thward.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/RPM-Flyover-1024x768.jpg)

### How will RPM benefit the 44th Ward?

The Red and Purple Modernization (RPM) corridor is a 9.6 mile stretch of track built over a century ago stretching from Belmont to Howard. It serves some of Chicago’s densest areas including Lakeview and the 44th Ward. In order to accommodate current and predicted increases in ridership along the RPM corridor during rush hours, the CTA needs to increase service, however it is currently at capacity. The RPM program addresses this issue by completely modernizing and rebuilding much of the century-old corridor from Belmont to Howard. In the 44th Ward, RPM will encompass the complete reconstruction of the Red and Purple Line track structures from Belmont to Cornelia/Newport (referred to as the North Main Line Reconstruction). Between Addison and Belmont, southbound Red and Purple line service will operate along the same northbound track; while, northbound Red and Purple Line service will operate along the same southbound track. This change is necessary for the dismantlement and replacement of the North Main Line’s western most tracks. A temporary track structure has been built to enable the continuation of normal service of the Loop-bound Brown Line as the normal track configuration is updated.

### What is the Red-Purple Bypass?

As part of the first phase of the RPM Program, CTA has completed construction of the Red-Purple Bypass directly north of the Belmont Station. The bypass has eliminated a bottleneck that previously prevented the CTA from adding more train service along the Red, Purple, and Brown Lines. The previous layout of the rail intersection required that all northbound Brown Line trains cross over the four tracks used by the Red and Purple Lines, interrupting and delaying Red and Purple Line trains as Brown Line trains crossed over. The new configuration enhances the efficiency of train operations, raising the amount of service the CTA can run along the entire Red, Purple, and Brown Lines. This enables the CTA to reduce overcrowding and meet growing demand for transit service. Benefits of the Red-Purple Bypass include:

*   **The addition of up to eight more Red Line trains per hour** during rush periods
*   **Ability to accommodate up to 7,200 additional customers per hour** during rush hour
*   **Increased Red and Purple line train speeds by 60 percent** through this intersection
*   **Customers are saved a half-million travel hours each year**

### ![Image 3](https://www.44thward.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/CTA-Track-Configuration-1.jpg)

### **Temporary Track Structure**

In order to continue to provide Red, Purple, and Brown Line service throughout RPM Phase One construction (2019-2025), a temporary track structure has been built parallel to the Red, Purple, and Brown Line tracks between Belmont Avenue and north of School Street. Trains will use this track for several years during construction.

**Project Timeline**

*   Spring 2018: Advance utility relocation work begins
*   December 2018: CTA selects Walsh-Fluor as design-build contractor
*   February 2019: CTA issued Notice to Proceed to Walsh-Fluor to begin project work
*   Winter 2019: Property demolition complete
*   End of 2019: Heavy civil work related to advance utility relocation to be substantially completed
*   October 2019: Major construction begins on Red-Purple Bypass with start of track foundation work
*   2021: Red-Purple Bypass to be completed
*   **2021 – 2024: CTA reconstruction of North Main lines (Red and Purple Line track structure reconstruction between Belmont and Cornelia/Newport)**
*   **End of 2024: North Main Line reconstruction to be completed.**

For more information on this project, please visit [https://www.transitchicago.com/rpm/](https://www.transitchicago.com/rpm/)

Red Ahead
=========

What is the Red Ahead program?
------------------------------

![Image 12: Building a New Chicago](https://www.transitchicago.com/assets/1/6/medium_buildinganewchicago.gif)The Red Ahead program is a comprehensive initiative for maintaining, modernizing, and expanding Chicago’s most-traveled rail line. The program includes three major improvement projects on the Red and Purple Lines between Linden terminal on the north and the proposed 130th Street terminal on the south. All three projects are mutually beneficial; an improvement in one area of the Red Line benefits the entire Red Line.

In addition, the Red Ahead program includes several individual projects, including the renovation of several individual stations along the Red Line.

  
From Linden to 130th
-----------------------

*   Over 240,000 CTA riders on an average weekday currently enter the system at stations in this corridor 
    *   This represents over 40% of all current CTA rail station entries 
*   Improvements would attract thousands in additional average weekday station entries 
    *   ~26 miles long 
    *   ~5 miles would be added by the extension
*   41 existing stations
    *   4 stations would be added by the extension
