| The first "L", the [Chicago and South Side Rapid Transit Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_and_South_Side_Rapid_Transit_Railroad "Chicago and South Side Rapid Transit Railroad"), began revenue service on June 6, 1892, when a steam locomotive pulling four wooden coaches, carrying more than a couple of dozen people, departed the 39th Street station and arrived at the [Congress Street Terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_Terminal "Congress Terminal") 14 minutes later,[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-running-16) over tracks that are still in use by the Green Line. Over the next year, service was extended to 63rd Street and [Stony Island Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stony_Island_Avenue "Stony Island Avenue"), then the Transportation Building of the [World's Columbian Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World%27s_Columbian_Exposition "World's Columbian Exposition") in [Jackson Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_Park_/(Chicago/) "Jackson Park (Chicago)").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-borzo-17) In 1893, trains began running on the [Lake Street Elevated Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Street_Elevated_Railroad "Lake Street Elevated Railroad") and in 1895 on the [Metropolitan West Side Elevated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_West_Side_Elevated_Railroad "Metropolitan West Side Elevated Railroad"), which had lines to Douglas Park, Garfield Park (since replaced), Humboldt Park (since demolished), and Logan Square. The Metropolitan was the United States' first non-exhibition rapid transit system powered by electric [traction motors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traction_motor "Traction motor"),[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-borzo-17) a technology whose practicality had been demonstrated in 1893 on the "intramural railway" at the [World's Columbian Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World%27s_Columbian_Exposition "World's Columbian Exposition") in Chicago.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-jasckson-18) Two years later the South Side "L" introduced [multiple-unit control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple-unit_train_control "Multiple-unit train control"), in which the operator can control all the motorized cars in a train, not just the lead unit. Electrification and MU control remain standard features of most of the world's rapid transit systems.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] A drawback of early "L" service was that none of the lines entered the central business district. Instead trains dropped passengers at stub terminals on the periphery due to a state law at the time requiring approval by neighboring property owners for tracks built over public streets, something not easily obtained downtown. This obstacle was overcome by the legendary traction magnate [Charles Tyson Yerkes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Yerkes "Charles Yerkes"), who went on to play a pivotal role in the development of the [London Underground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Underground "London Underground"), and who was immortalized by [Theodore Dreiser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Dreiser "Theodore Dreiser") as the ruthless schemer Frank Cowperwood in _[The Titan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Titan_/(novel/) "The Titan (novel)")_ (1914) and other novels.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-Kamin2020-19) Yerkes, who controlled much of the city's [streetcar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streetcar "Streetcar") system, obtained the necessary signatures through cash and guile—at one point he secured a franchise to build a mile-long "L" over Van Buren Street from Wabash Avenue to Halsted Street, extracting the requisite majority from the pliable owners on the western half of the route, then building tracks chiefly over the eastern half, where property owners had opposed him. Designed by noted bridge builder [John Alexander Low Waddell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Alexander_Low_Waddell "John Alexander Low Waddell"), the elevated tracks used a multiple close-rivet system to withstand the forces of the passing trains' kinetic energy.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-Kamin2020-19) The Union Loop opened in 1897 and greatly increased the rapid transit system's convenience. Operation on the Yerkes-owned [Northwestern Elevated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwestern_Elevated_Railroad "Northwestern Elevated Railroad"), which built the North Side "L" lines, began three years later, essentially completing the elevated infrastructure in the urban core although extensions and branches continued to be constructed in outlying areas through the 1920s.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] After 1911, the "L" lines came under the control of [Samuel Insull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Insull "Samuel Insull"), president of the Chicago Edison electric utility (now [Commonwealth Edison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Edison "Commonwealth Edison")), whose interest stemmed initially from the fact that the trains were the city's largest consumer of electricity. Insull instituted many improvements, including free transfers and through routing, although he did not formally combine the original firms into the [Chicago Rapid Transit Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Rapid_Transit_Company "Chicago Rapid Transit Company") until 1924. He also bought three other Chicago electrified railroads, the [Chicago North Shore and Milwaukee Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_North_Shore_and_Milwaukee_Railroad "Chicago North Shore and Milwaukee Railroad"), [Chicago Aurora and Elgin Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Aurora_and_Elgin_Railroad "Chicago Aurora and Elgin Railroad"), and [South Shore Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Shore_Line "South Shore Line") [interurban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interurban "Interurban") lines, and ran the trains of the first two into downtown Chicago via the "L" tracks.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-Kamin2020-19) This period of relative prosperity ended when Insull's empire collapsed in 1932, but later in the decade the city, with the help of the federal government, accumulated sufficient funds to begin construction of two subway lines to supplement and, some hoped, permit eventual replacement of the Loop elevated; as early as the 1920s some city leaders wanted to replace the "ugly" elevated tracks. These plans advanced in the 1970s under mayors [Richard J. Daley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_J._Daley "Richard J. Daley") and [Michael Bilandic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_A._Bilandic "Michael A. Bilandic") until a public outcry against tearing down the popular "L" began, led by _Chicago Tribune_ columnist [Paul Gapp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Gapp "Paul Gapp") and architect [Harry Weese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Weese "Harry Weese"). Instead, then new Mayor [Jane Byrne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Byrne "Jane Byrne") protected the elevated lines and directed their rehabilitation.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-Kamin2020-19) The State Street subway opened on October 17, 1943.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-state-20)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-subway-21) The Dearborn Subway, on which work had been suspended during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), opened on February 25, 1951.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-dearborn-22) The subways were constructed with a secondary purpose of serving as bomb shelters, as evidenced by the close spacing of the support columns (a more extensive plan proposed replacing the entire elevated system with subways). In 1947, the Chicago Transit Authority (CTA) acquired the assets of the Chicago Rapid Transit Company and the [Chicago Surface Lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Surface_Lines "Chicago Surface Lines"), operator of the city's streetcars. Over the next few years CTA modernized the "L", replacing wooden cars with new steel ones and closing lightly used branch lines and [stations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_closed_Chicago_%27L%27_stations "List of closed Chicago 'L' stations"), many of which had been spaced only a quarter-mile apart.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] Rail service to O'Hare International Airport first opened in 1984 and to Midway International Airport in 1993. That same year, the CTA renamed all of its rail lines; they are now identified by color.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-CBS-fast-facts-10) The CTA introduced fare cards for the first time in 1997. [![Image 1541](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/20090503_under_Chicago_L_on_Franklin_Street.jpg/250px-20090503_under_Chicago_L_on_Franklin_Street.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:20090503_under_Chicago_L_on_Franklin_Street.jpg) The [Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_Line_/(CTA/) "Brown Line (CTA)") and [Purple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple_Line_/(CTA/) "Purple Line (CTA)") Chicago "L" lines run above vehicular traffic on Franklin Street in the [Near North Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near_North_Side,_Chicago "Near North Side, Chicago") [community area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_areas_of_Chicago "Community areas of Chicago"). Later, after assuming control of the "L", the CTA introduced A/B skip-stop service. Under this service, trains were designated as either "A" or "B" trains, and stations were alternately designated as "A" stations or "B" stations, with heavily used stations designated as both – "AB". "A" trains would stop only at "A" and "AB" stations, and "B" trains would stop only at "B" and "AB" stations. Station signage carried the station's skip-stop letter and was also color-coded by skip-stop type; "A" stations had red signage, "B" stations had green signage, and "AB" stations had blue signage. The system was designed to speed up lines by having trains skip stations while still allowing for frequent service at the heavily used "AB" stations. A/B skip-stop service debuted on the Lake Street Elevated in 1948, and the service proved effective as travel times were cut by a third. By the 1950s, the service was used throughout the system. All lines used the A/B skip-stop service between the 1950s and the 1990s with the exception of the Evanston and Skokie lines, which were suburban-only lines and did not justify skip-stop service. On the lines with branches, skip-stop service sent all "A" trains to one branch and "B" trains to another branch. On what became the Blue Line, "A" trains were routed on the Congress branch while "B" trains were sent to the Douglas branch. On the North-South Line, "A" trains went to the Englewood branch and "B" trains went to the Jackson Park branch. In both cases, individual stops were not skipped beyond the points where those branches diverged. As time went by, the time periods which employed skip-stop service gradually decreased, as the waits at "A" and "B" stations became increasingly longer during non-peak service. By the 1990s, use of the A/B skip-stop system was only used during rush hour service. Another problem was that trains skipping stations to save time still could not pass the train that was directly ahead, so skipping stations was not advantageous in all regards. In 1993, the CTA began to eliminate skip-stop service when it switched the southern branches of the West-South and North-South Lines to improve rider efficiency, creating the current Red and Green Lines. From this point, Green Line trains made all stops along the entire route, while Red Line trains stopped at all stations south of [Harrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrison_/(CTA_station/) "Harrison (CTA station)"). The elimination of A/B skip-stop service continued with the opening of the all-stop Orange Line and the conversion of the Brown Line to all-stop service.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-skipstop-23) In April 1995, the last of the A/B skip-stop system was eliminated with the conversion of the O'Hare branch of the Blue Line and the Howard branch of the Red Line to all-stop service. The removal of skip-stop service resulted in some increases in travel times, and greatly increased ridership at former "A" and "B" stations due to increased train frequencies. Station signage highlighting the former skip-stop patterns would remain into the 2000s, when it was gradually replaced across the system.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-skipstop-23) The first air-conditioned cars were introduced in 1964. The last pre–World War II cars were retired in 1973. New lines were built in expressway medians, a technique implemented in Chicago and followed by other cities worldwide. The Congress branch, built in the median of the Eisenhower Expressway, replaced the Garfield Park "L" in 1958. The Dan Ryan branch, built in the median of the Dan Ryan Expressway, opened on September 28, 1969,[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-ryan-24) followed by an extension of the Milwaukee elevated into the Kennedy Expressway in 1970. As of 2014, Chicago "L" trains run over a total of 224.1 miles (360.7 km) of track.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-CTA_facts-1) [![Image 1542](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/JacksonStation_RedLine_CTA.jpg/250px-JacksonStation_RedLine_CTA.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:JacksonStation_RedLine_CTA.jpg) The Jackson/State subway stop on the Red Line (2004) Ridership has been growing steadily after the CTA takeover despite declining mass transit usage nationwide, with an average of 594,000 riders boarding each weekday in 1960[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-25) and 759,866 in 2016 (or 47% of all CTA rides).[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-CBS-fast-facts-10) Due to the [Loop Flood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_flood "Chicago flood") in April 1992, ridership was at 418,000 that year[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-26) because CTA was forced to suspend operation for several weeks in both the State and [Dearborn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milwaukee%E2%80%93Dearborn_subway "Milwaukee–Dearborn subway") subways, used by the most heavily traveled lines. Growing ridership has not been uniformly distributed. Use of North Side lines is heavy and continues to grow, while that of West Side and South Side lines tend to remain stable. Ridership on the North Side Brown Line, for instance, has increased 83% since 1979, necessitating a station reconstruction project to accommodate longer trains.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-brown-27) [![Image 1543](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/CTA_waiting_on_the_platform.jpg/250px-CTA_waiting_on_the_platform.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CTA_waiting_on_the_platform.jpg) A Red Line train pulls into Adams/Wabash, being rerouted over elevated tracks due to construction in the State Street subway (2007) Annual traffic on the Howard branch of the Red Line, which reached 38.7 million in 2010 and 40.9 million in 2011, has exceeded the 1927 prewar peak of 38.5 million.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-28) The section of the Blue Line between the Loop and [Logan Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logan_Square,_Chicago "Logan Square, Chicago"), which serves once-neglected but now bustling neighborhoods such as [Wicker Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wicker_Park,_Chicago "Wicker Park, Chicago"), [Bucktown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bucktown,_Chicago "Bucktown, Chicago"), and [Palmer Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmer_Square,_Chicago "Palmer Square, Chicago"), has seen a 54% increase in weekday riders since 1992. On the other hand, weekday ridership on the South Side portion of the Green Line, which closed for two years for reconstruction from January 1994 to May 1996, was 50,400 in 1978 but only 13,000 in 2006. Boardings at the 95th/Dan Ryan stop on the Red Line, though still among the system's busiest at 11,100 riders per weekday[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-29) as of February 2015, are less than half the peak volume in the 1980s. In 1976, three North Side "L" branches – what were then known as the Howard, Milwaukee, and Ravenswood lines − accounted for 42% of non-downtown boardings. Today (with the help of the Blue Line extension to O'Hare), they account for 58%.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] The North Side, which has historically been the highest density area of the city, reflects the Chicago building boom between 2000 and 2010, which has focused primarily on North Side neighborhoods and downtown.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-northshore-30) It may ease somewhat in the wake of the current high level of residential construction along the south lakefront. For example, ridership at the linked Roosevelt stops on the Green, Orange, and Red Lines,[\[note 3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-31) which serve the burgeoning [South Loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near_South_Side,_Chicago "Near South Side, Chicago") neighborhood, has tripled since 1992, with an average of 8,000 boardings per weekday. Patronage at the Cermak-[Chinatown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinatown,_Chicago "Chinatown, Chicago") stop on the Red Line, with 4,000 weekday boardings, is at the highest level since the station opened in 1969. The 2003 _Chicago Central Area Plan_ proposed construction of a [Green Line station at Cermak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cermak%E2%80%93McCormick_Place_/(CTA_station/) "Cermak–McCormick Place (CTA station)"), between Chinatown and the [McCormick Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCormick_Place "McCormick Place") convention center, in expectation of continued density growth in the vicinity. This station opened in 2015. Ventra also works with CTA buses, [Pace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pace_/(transit/) "Pace (transit)") (suburban buses), and [Metra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metra "Metra") (commuter rail). Payment by a smartphone app, the Ventra app, or by a contactless bankcard is possible.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-37) As of 2018, the "L" uses a flat fare of $2.50 for almost the entire system, the only exception being [O'Hare International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O%27Hare_/(CTA_station/) "O'Hare (CTA station)") on the Blue Line, at which passengers entering the station are charged a higher fare of $5.00 (passengers leaving the system at this station are not charged this higher fare).[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-ReferenceA-38) The higher fare is being charged for what the CTA considers "premium-level" service to O'Hare.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-Chicago_Tribune-39) Use of the [Midway International Airport Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midway_/(CTA_station/) "Midway (CTA station)") does not require this higher fare; it only requires the $2.50 regular fare.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-ReferenceA-38) The higher charge at O'Hare has been the source of some controversy in recent years, because of the CTA's plan to eliminate the exemption from the premium fare for airport workers, [Transportation Security Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_Security_Administration "Transportation Security Administration") workers, and airline workers.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-Chicago_Tribune-39) After protests from those groups, the CTA extended the exemptions for six months.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-40) [![Image 1545](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/CTA_Night.jpg/250px-CTA_Night.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CTA_Night.jpg) A view of the Chicago "L" in the [Loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Loop "Chicago Loop") (2009) [![Image 1546](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/CTA_loop_junction.jpg/250px-CTA_loop_junction.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CTA_loop_junction.jpg) [![Image 1547](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/Gerald_Farinas_Central_Street_CTA_Station.jpg/250px-Gerald_Farinas_Central_Street_CTA_Station.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gerald_Farinas_Central_Street_CTA_Station.jpg) The Purple Line serves [Evanston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evanston,_Illinois "Evanston, Illinois") and [Wilmette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilmette,_Illinois "Wilmette, Illinois") with weekday rush-hour express service to downtown Chicago (2006). [![Image 1548](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/McCormick_Tribune_060304.jpg/250px-McCormick_Tribune_060304.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:McCormick_Tribune_060304.jpg) [![Image 1549](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Jackson_Station.jpg/250px-Jackson_Station.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jackson_Station.jpg) Since 1993, "L" lines have been officially identified by color,[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-L_CTA_Chron-41) although older route names survive to some extent in CTA publications and popular usage to distinguish branches of longer lines. Stations are found throughout Chicago, as well as in the suburbs of [Forest Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_Park,_Illinois "Forest Park, Illinois"), [Oak Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oak_Park,_Illinois "Oak Park, Illinois"), [Evanston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evanston,_Illinois "Evanston, Illinois"), [Wilmette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilmette,_Illinois "Wilmette, Illinois"), [Cicero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicero,_Illinois "Cicero, Illinois"), [Rosemont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosemont,_Illinois "Rosemont, Illinois"), and [Skokie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skokie,_Illinois "Skokie, Illinois").      **[Blue Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Line_/(CTA/) "Blue Line (CTA)")**, consisting of the _O'Hare_, _[Milwaukee–Dearborn subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milwaukee%E2%80%93Dearborn_subway "Milwaukee–Dearborn subway")_, and _Congress_ branches The Blue Line extends from [O'Hare International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O%27Hare_International_Airport "O'Hare International Airport") through the [Loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Loop_/(CTA/) "The Loop (CTA)") via the Milwaukee-Dearborn subway to the West Side. Trains travel to [Des Plaines Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_Park_/(CTA_station/) "Forest Park (CTA station)") in [Forest Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_Park,_Illinois "Forest Park, Illinois") via the [Eisenhower Expressway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_290_/(Illinois/) "Interstate 290 (Illinois)") median. The route from O'Hare to Forest Park is 26.93 miles (43 km) long, with 33 stations. Until 1970, the northern section of the Blue Line terminated at [Logan Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logan_Square_station_/(CTA_Logan_Square_branch/) "Logan Square station (CTA Logan Square branch)"). During that time, the line was called the **Milwaukee** route after [Milwaukee Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milwaukee_Avenue_/(Chicago/) "Milwaukee Avenue (Chicago)"), which runs parallel to it; in that year, service was extended to [Jefferson Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_Park_Transit_Center "Jefferson Park Transit Center") via the [Kennedy Expressway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Expressway "Kennedy Expressway") median, and in 1984 to [O'Hare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O%27Hare_/(CTA_station/) "O'Hare (CTA station)"). The Blue Line is the second-busiest, with 176,120 weekday boardings.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-2013_ridership-42) It operates [24 hours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/24/7_service "24/7 service") a day, 7 days a week.      **[Brown Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_Line_/(CTA/) "Brown Line (CTA)")** or _[Ravenswood branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ravenswood_branch "Ravenswood branch")_ The Brown Line follows an 11.4-mile (18 km) route, between the [Kimball terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kimball_station "Kimball station") in [Albany Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albany_Park,_Chicago "Albany Park, Chicago") and the Loop in [downtown Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Loop "Chicago Loop"). In 2013, the Brown Line had an average weekday ridership of 108,529.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-2013_ridership-42)      **[Green Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Line_/(CTA/) "Green Line (CTA)")**, consisting of the _[Lake Street Elevated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Street_Elevated "Lake Street Elevated")_, _[South Side Elevated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Side_Elevated "South Side Elevated")_, _[Ashland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashland_branch "Ashland branch")_, and _[East 63rd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_63rd_branch "East 63rd branch")_ branches A completely elevated route utilizing the system's oldest segments (dating back to 1892), the Green Line extends 20.8 miles (33.5 km) with 30 stops between Forest Park and [Oak Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oak_Park,_Illinois "Oak Park, Illinois") ([Harlem/Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem/Lake_/(CTA_station/) "Harlem/Lake (CTA station)")), through The Loop, to the South Side. South of the Garfield station the line splits into two branches, with trains terminating at [Ashland/63rd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashland/63rd_/(CTA_station/) "Ashland/63rd (CTA station)") in [West Englewood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Englewood,_Chicago "West Englewood, Chicago") and terminating at [Cottage Grove/63rd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cottage_Grove_/(CTA_station/) "Cottage Grove (CTA station)") in [Woodlawn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodlawn,_Chicago "Woodlawn, Chicago"). The East 63rd branch formerly extended to [Jackson Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_Park_/(CTA_station/) "Jackson Park (CTA station)"), but the portion of the line east of Cottage Grove, which ran above 63rd Street, was demolished in the 1980s and 1997 due to structural problems and was never rebuilt due to community demands. The average number of weekday boardings in 2013 was 68,230.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-2013_ridership-42)      **[Orange Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orange_Line_/(CTA/) "Orange Line (CTA)")** or _Midway Line_ The 13-mile (21 km) long Orange Line was constructed from 1987 until 1993 on existing railroad embankments and new concrete and steel elevated structure. It runs from a [station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midway_/(CTA_station/) "Midway (CTA station)") adjacent to [Midway International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midway_International_Airport "Midway International Airport") on the Southwest Side to The Loop in downtown Chicago. Average weekday ridership in 2013 was 58,765.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-2013_ridership-42)      **[Pink Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pink_Line_/(CTA/) "Pink Line (CTA)")** consisting of the _[Cermak branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cermak_branch "Cermak branch")_ and _[Paulina connector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logan_Square_branch#Paulina_Connector "Logan Square branch")_ The Pink Line is an 11.2-mile (18 km) rerouting of former Blue Line branch trains from [54th/Cermak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th/Cermak_/(CTA_station/) "54th/Cermak (CTA station)") in [Cicero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicero,_Illinois "Cicero, Illinois") via the previously non-revenue Paulina Connector and the Green Line on Lake Street to the Loop. Its average weekday ridership in 2013 was 31,572.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-2013_ridership-42) The branch formerly ran to Oak Park Avenue in Berwyn, 2.1 miles (3.4 km) west of its current terminal. In 1952, service on the portion of the line west of 54th Avenue closed and, over the next decade, the stations and tracks were demolished. The street level right-of-way is used to this day as parking, locally known as the " 'L' Strip".[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-43)      **[Purple Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple_Line_/(CTA/) "Purple Line (CTA)")**, consisting of the _Evanston Shuttle_ and _Evanston Express_ The Purple Line is a 3.9-mile (6 km) branch serving north suburban Evanston and Wilmette with express service to the Loop during weekday rush hours. The local service operates from the [Linden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linden_/(CTA_station/) "Linden (CTA station)") terminal in [Wilmette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilmette,_Illinois "Wilmette, Illinois") through Evanston to the [Howard terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_/(CTA_station/) "Howard (CTA station)") on the north side of Chicago where it connects with the Red and Yellow lines. The weekday rush-hour express service continues from Howard to the Loop, running nonstop on the four-track line used by the Red Line to [Wilson station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_station_/(CTA/) "Wilson station (CTA)"), then serving [Belmont station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_/(CTA_North_Side_Main_Line_station/) "Belmont (CTA North Side Main Line station)"), followed by all Brown Line stops to the Loop. Its 2013 average weekday ridership was 42,673 passenger boardings.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-2013_ridership-42) The stops from Belmont to [Chicago Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_/(CTA_Brown_and_Purple_Lines_station/) "Chicago (CTA Brown and Purple Lines station)") were added in the 1990s to relieve crowding on the Red and Brown lines.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-44) Its purple color is a reference to nearby [Northwestern University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwestern_University "Northwestern University"), with four stops (Davis, Foster, Noyes, and Central) located just two blocks west of the university campus.      **[Red Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Line_/(CTA/) "Red Line (CTA)")**, consisting of the _[North Side main line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Side_main_line "North Side main line")_, _[State Street subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Street_subway "State Street subway")_, and _[Dan Ryan branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Ryan_branch "Dan Ryan branch")_ The Red Line is the busiest route, with 234,232 passenger boardings on an average weekday in 2013.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-2013_ridership-42) It includes 33 stations on its 26-mile (42 km) route, traveling from the [Howard terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_/(CTA_station/) "Howard (CTA station)") on the city's north side, through downtown Chicago via the [State Street subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Street_subway "State Street subway"), then down the [Dan Ryan Expressway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Ryan_Expressway "Dan Ryan Expressway") median to [95th/Dan Ryan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/95th/Dan_Ryan_/(CTA_station/) "95th/Dan Ryan (CTA station)") on the [South Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roseland,_Chicago "Roseland, Chicago"). Despite its length, the Red Line stops 5 miles (8.0 km) short of the city's southern border. Extension plans to 130th Street are currently being considered. The Red Line is one of two lines operating [24 hours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/24/7_service "24/7 service") a day, seven days a week and is the only CTA "L" line that goes to both [Wrigley Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wrigley_Field "Wrigley Field") and [Rate Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rate_Field "Rate Field"), the homes of Chicago's Major League Baseball teams, the [Chicago Cubs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Cubs "Chicago Cubs") and [Chicago White Sox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_White_Sox "Chicago White Sox"). Rail cars are stored at the **[Howard Yard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Yard "Howard Yard")** on the north end of the line and at the **[98th Yard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/98th_Yard "98th Yard")** at the south end.      **[Yellow Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_Line_/(CTA/) "Yellow Line (CTA)")**, or _Skokie Swift_ The Yellow Line is a 4.7-mile (8 km) three-station line that runs from the [Howard Street terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_/(CTA_station/) "Howard (CTA station)") to the [Dempster–Skokie terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dempster%E2%80%93Skokie_station "Dempster–Skokie station") in north suburban [Skokie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skokie,_Illinois "Skokie, Illinois"). The Yellow Line is the only "L" route that does not provide direct service to the Loop. This line was originally part of the [North Shore Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_North_Shore_and_Milwaukee_Railroad "Chicago North Shore and Milwaukee Railroad")'s rail service, and was acquired by the CTA in the 1960s. The Yellow Line previously operated as a nonstop [shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_train "Shuttle train"), until the downtown Skokie station [Oakton–Skokie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oakton%E2%80%93Skokie_/(CTA_station/) "Oakton–Skokie (CTA station)") opened on April 30, 2012.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-45) Its average weekday ridership in 2013 was 6,338 passenger boardings.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-2013_ridership-42) _[The Loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Loop_/(CTA/) "The Loop (CTA)")_ Brown, Green, Orange, Pink, and Purple Line Express trains serve downtown Chicago via the Loop elevated. The Loop's eight stations average 72,843 weekday boardings. The Orange Line, Purple Line and the Pink Line run clockwise; the Brown Line runs counter-clockwise. The Green Line runs in both directions through the north and east sides; the other four lines circle the Loop and return to their starting points. The Loop forms a rectangle roughly 0.4 miles (640 m) long east-to-west and 0.6 miles (970 m) long north-to-south. The Loop [three-quarter union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_union "Grand union") at Lake and Wells has been described in the _[Guinness Book of World Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinness_World_Records "Guinness World Records")_ as the world's busiest railroad crossing.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] [![Image 1550](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/ba/CTA_2842_7-17-94.jpg/250px-CTA_2842_7-17-94.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CTA_2842_7-17-94.jpg) [![Image 1551](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Chicago_Elevated_Train.jpg/250px-Chicago_Elevated_Train.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chicago_Elevated_Train.jpg) A 4-car train of 3200-series cars pulls into [State/Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State/Lake_/(CTA_station/) "State/Lake (CTA station)") (2006) [![Image 1552](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/93/New_CTA_Series_5000_Series_Cars.jpg/250px-New_CTA_Series_5000_Series_Cars.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:New_CTA_Series_5000_Series_Cars.jpg) The CTA operates over 1,350 "L" cars,[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-CTA_facts-1) divided among four series, all of which are semi-permanently coupled into married pairs. All cars on the system utilize 600-[volt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volt "Volt") [direct current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_current "Direct current") power delivered through a [third rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_rail "Third rail"). The [2600-series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2600-series_/(CTA/) "2600-series (CTA)") was built from 1981 until 1987 by the [Budd Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budd_Company "Budd Company") of [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"), Pennsylvania. After the completion of the order of the 2600-series cars, Budd changed its name to Transit America and ceased production of railcars. With 509 cars in operation, the 2600-series is the largest of the three series of "L" cars in operation. The cars were rebuilt by [Alstom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alstom "Alstom") of [Hornell, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hornell,_New_York "Hornell, New York"), from 1999 until 2002. The [3200-series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3200-series_/(CTA/) "3200-series (CTA)"), was built from 1992 until 1994 by [Morrison-Knudsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrison-Knudsen "Morrison-Knudsen") of Hornell, New York. These cars have fluted, stainless steel sides similar to the now-retired [2200-series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2200-series_/(CTA/) "2200-series (CTA)"). The [5000-series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000-series_/(CTA/) "5000-series (CTA)") train cars are equipped with [AC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternating_current "Alternating current") propulsion; interior security cameras; aisle-facing seating, which allow for greater passenger capacity; [LED](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light-emitting_diode "Light-emitting diode") destination signs, interior readouts, and interior maps; GPS; glow-in-the-dark evacuation signs; operator-controlled ventilation systems; among other features. AC propulsion allows for smoother acceleration, lower operational costs, less wear and tear, and greater energy efficiency. The AC propulsion can take advantage of [regenerative braking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regenerative_brake "Regenerative brake"), meaning the train returns excess energy to the third rail as it slows down.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-46) With the DC propulsion of the previous series, they utilize dynamic braking which converts the excess kinetic energy into heat within a resistor bank. Next-generation train cars, the [7000-series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7000-series_/(CTA/) "7000-series (CTA)"), have been ordered and are beginning to enter service. Each 7000-series rail car will feature LEDs, 37 to 38 seats, and is a hybrid of the 3200-series and 5000-series.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-47) The design and arrangement of seats were modified to improve ergonomics and increase leg room. Enhanced air conditioning will circulate air more efficiently during hot summer days. Laser sensors above the doors will count the number of passengers, allowing the CTA to track passenger volumes and change its schedules accordingly.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-48) State-owned manufacturer CRRC Sifang America (China Rail Rolling Stock Corporation) won the contract, besting the other major competitor, Bombardier from Canada by $226 million. Concerns have been raised over possible malware, cyber attacks, and mass surveillance by the Chinese government. The computer and software components and the automatic train control system will be made by U.S. and Canadian firms.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-49) The cars are being built at a new CRRC Sifang America rail car manufacturing plant at 13535 South Torrence Avenue in Chicago's [Hegewisch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hegewisch,_Chicago "Hegewisch, Chicago") neighborhood.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-first-step-50) Production of the 7000-series cars commenced in June 2019.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-:02-51)[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-52)[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-53) This is the first time in more than 50 years CTA rail cars are manufactured in Chicago.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-first-step-50)[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-54) Ten cars in the 7000-series began testing revenue service on April 21, 2021.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-:5-55) The base order is for 400 cars and will be used to replace the [2600-series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2600-series_/(CTA/) "2600-series (CTA)") cars.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-:12-56) If the CTA ordered the additional 446 cars, they would also replace the [3200-series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3200-series_/(CTA/) "3200-series (CTA)") cars.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-57) In May 2023, the CTA announced it has received $200 million funding from the Federal Transit Authority; this money will go towards the development of the [9000-series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9000-series_/(CTA/) "9000-series (CTA)") rail cars. The plan is to acquire up to 300 new train sets.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-58) [![Image 1553](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/20220113_03a_CTA_Green_Line_L_near_Congress_St.jpg/250px-20220113_03a_CTA_Green_Line_L_near_Congress_St.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:20220113_03a_CTA_Green_Line_L_near_Congress_St.jpg) A 7000-series train being tested on the Green Line near Congress Street (2022) Chicago's rapid-transit system is officially nicknamed the "L".[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-59) This name for the CTA rail system applies to the whole system: its elevated, subway, at-grade, and open-cut segments. The use of the nickname dates from the earliest days of the elevated railroads. Newspapers of the late 1880s referred to proposed elevated railroads in Chicago as "'L' roads."[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-60) The first route to be constructed, the [Chicago and South Side Rapid Transit Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_and_South_Side_Rapid_Transit_Railroad "Chicago and South Side Rapid Transit Railroad") gained the nickname "Alley Elevated", or "Alley L" during its planning and construction,[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-61) a term that was widely used by 1893, less than a year after the line opened.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-62)[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-63) In discussing various stylings of "Loop" and "L" in _Destination Loop: The Story of Rapid Transit Railroading in and around Chicago_ (1982), author Brian J. Cudahy quotes a passage from _[The Neon Wilderness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Neon_Wilderness "The Neon Wilderness")_ (1947) by Chicago author [Nelson Algren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Algren "Nelson Algren"): "beneath the curved steel of the El, beneath the endless ties." Cudahy then comments, "Note that in the quotation above ... it says 'El' to mean 'elevated rapid transit railroad.' We trust that this usage can be ascribed to a publisher's editor in New York or some other east coast city; in Chicago the same expression is routinely rendered 'L'." As used by CTA, the name is rendered as the capital letter 'L', in single quotation marks. "L" (with double quotation marks) was often used by CTA predecessors such as the Chicago Rapid Transit Company; however, the CTA uses single quotation marks (') on some printed materials and signs rather than double. In Chicago, the term "subway" only applies to the [State Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Street_subway "State Street subway") and [Milwaukee–Dearborn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milwaukee%E2%80%93Dearborn_subway "Milwaukee–Dearborn subway") subways and is not applied to the system as a whole, unlike in New York City where both the elevated and underground portions make up the [New York City Subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Subway "New York City Subway"). Renovation and expansion plans ------------------------------ \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chicago_%22L%22&action=edit§ion=14 "Edit section: Renovation and expansion plans")\] Like other large and aging rapid transit systems, the Chicago "L" faces problems of delays, breakdowns, and a multi-billion-dollar backlog of deferred maintenance.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-:1-64) The CTA is currently focused on eliminating slow zones, modernizing the Red, Blue, and Purple lines, and improving "L" stations. In addition, CTA has studied numerous other proposals for expanded rail service and renovations, some of which may be implemented in the future.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-65) ### Recent service improvements and capital projects \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chicago_%22L%22&action=edit§ion=15 "Edit section: Recent service improvements and capital projects")\] [![Image 1554](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/00/LaSalle_Van_Buren_060626.jpg/250px-LaSalle_Van_Buren_060626.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:LaSalle_Van_Buren_060626.jpg) "L" train wrapped in pink to mark the start of the Pink Line trial service During the 2000s and 2010s, the CTA has completed several renovation and new construction projects.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-66) Pink Line service began on June 25, 2006, though it did not include any new tracks or stations. The Pink Line travels over what was formerly a branch of the Blue Line from the 54th/Cermak terminal in [Cicero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicero,_Illinois "Cicero, Illinois") to the Polk station in Chicago. Pink Line trains then proceed via the Paulina Connector to the Lake Street branch of the Green Line and then clockwise around the Loop elevated via Lake-Wabash-Van Buren-Wells. Douglas trains used the same route between April 4, 1954, and June 22, 1958, after the old Garfield Park "L" line was demolished to make way for the Eisenhower Expressway.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-L_CTA_Chron-41) The new route, which serves 22 stations, offered more frequent service for riders on both the Congress and Douglas branches. Pink Line trains could be scheduled independently of Blue Line trains, and ran more frequently than the Douglas branch of the Blue Line did.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-pink-67) [![Image 1555](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/75/Fullerton_CTA_071208.jpg/250px-Fullerton_CTA_071208.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fullerton_CTA_071208.jpg) Fullerton station on the North Side for the Red, Brown, and Purple Lines, midway through reconstruction in December 2007 In late 2007, trains were forced to operate at reduced speed over more than 22% of the system due to deteriorated track, structure, and other problems.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-68) By October 2008, system-wide slow zones had been reduced to 9.1%[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-69) and by January 2010, total slow zones were reduced to 6.3%.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] CTA's Slow Zone Elimination Project is an ongoing effort to restore track work to conditions where trains no longer have to reduce speeds through deteriorating areas. The Loop received track work in 2012–2013. The Purple Line in Evanston received track work and viaduct replacement in 2011–2013. The Green Line Ashland branch received track work in 2013, prior to the Red Line Dan Ryan branch reconstruction.[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-CTA_Putting_Rapid_Back_in_Transit-70) The Brown Line Capacity Expansion Project enabled CTA to run eight-car trains on the Brown Line, and rebuilt stations to modern standards, including accessibility.[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-expansion-71) Before the project, Brown Line platforms could only accommodate six-car trains, and increasing ridership led to uncomfortably crowded trains. After several years of construction, eight-car trains began to run at rush hour on the Brown Line in April 2008. The project was completed in December 2009, on time and on budget, with only minor [punch list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punch_list "Punch list") work remaining. The project's total cost was expected to be around $530 million.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-72) While various mayors of Chicago had recognized the importance of reliable public transit, [Rahm Emanuel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rahm_Emanuel "Rahm Emanuel") received credit for making improving service a top priority. In addition to local funding, he managed to secure federal dollars by lobbying.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-:1-64) One of the largest reconstruction projects in the CTA's history, at a cost of $425 million, was the [Red Line South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Ahead#Red_Line_South_Reconstruction_project "Red Ahead") reconstruction project. From May 19, 2013, through October 20, 2013, the project closed and rebuilt the entire Dan Ryan branch—replacing and rebuilding all the tracks, ties, ballast and drainage systems—from Cermak-Chinatown to 95th/Dan Ryan.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-CTA_Red_South_Reconstruction-73) The station work involved renewing and improving eight stations, including new paint and lights, bus bridge improvements, new elevators at the Garfield, 63rd, and 87th stations and new roofs and canopies at some stations. "We are looking forward to providing our south Red Line customers with improved stations that are cleaner, brighter and better than they have been in years," said CTA President [Forrest Claypool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forrest_Claypool "Forrest Claypool").[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-Progressive_Railroading-74) Shutting down a portion of the railway instead of relegating work to the weekends enabled the project to be completed in months rather than years.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-:1-64) In 2014, the CTA initiated station and track upgrades on the Blue Line between Grand and O'Hare. This $492 million project has modernized stations (some of which were originally built in 1895), rebuilt tracks, replaced station platforms, upgraded water utilities, installed public art, and improved access to some stations (by adding elevators).[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-CTA_Your_New_Blue-75) This project, nearing completion as of 2022, is expected to cut travel time between the Loop and O'Hare by ten minutes.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-:1-64) In late 2015, extensive [4G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4G "4G") wireless coverage was added to both Blue and Red Line subways, with the $32.5 million installation cost paid for by [T-Mobile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-Mobile_US "T-Mobile US"), [Sprint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sprint_Corporation "Sprint Corporation"), [AT&T](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AT%26T "AT&T") and [Verizon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verizon "Verizon"). Upon the project's completion, Chicago became the largest American city with 4G Internet service in all of its subways and tunnels, a total of 22 miles (35 km). Besides adding to passenger convenience, it also improved security by allowing CTA personnel and first responders to communicate more easily in case of an emergency.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-76) [![Image 1556](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/Wilson_Station.jpg/250px-Wilson_Station.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wilson_Station.jpg) The newly rebuilt Wilson Station, September 2017 The new [Wilson Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_station_/(CTA/) "Wilson station (CTA)") officially reopened in October 2017. The century-old station now includes accessible elevators, escalators, new security cameras, three entrances, wider stairwells, additional turnstiles, larger platforms, new lights and signage, as well as bus and train trackers.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-77)[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-78)[\[note 4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-79) FastTracks is a program intended to address the slow zones and to make train rides smoother and more reliable. In order to achieve this, crews would replace worn tracks, rail ties, and ballasts. An upgraded power system along the O'Hare Blue Line branch would enable more trains to operate during peak periods. The Blue, Brown, Green, and Red lines would be worked on. This program was set to begin in early 2018 and would continue through 2021. Funding for this $179 million project comes from a fee increase imposed on [mobile app](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_app "Mobile app")\-based [vehicle for hire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vehicle_for_hire "Vehicle for hire") companies in Chicago, the first of its kind in the country.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-80) In Mayor Emanuel's 2018 budget proposal, the fee went from 52 cents to 67 cents per trip.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-81) First introduced in 2015, this fee rose by another five cents in 2019.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-82) In December 2018, The CTA Board approved $2.1 billion worth of contracts for the [modernization of the Red and Purple Lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Purple_Modernization_Project "Red and Purple Modernization Project"). The largest and most expensive in CTA history, this project includes the reconstruction of the junction between the Brown Line and Red/Purple line into a [flying junction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_junction "Flying junction") to reduce delays, and the reconstruction of the Lawrence, Argyle, Berwyn, and Bryn Mawr stations.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-NBC-redpurple-83) Construction of the project began on October 2, 2019, and is scheduled for completion in 2025.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-84) $100 million in federal funding for the reconstruction of the Red Line was approved September 2019. In the final days of the Barack Obama administration, the federal government agreed to provide $957 million in funding in total; the rest would come from a tax hike on property owners who lived within 0.5 miles (800 m) of the Red Line.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-85) Google announced in November 2024 that it would pay for the redesign of the [Clark/Lake station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark/Lake_station "Clark/Lake station") in a project related to the company's new Chicago headquarters at the former [Thompson Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_R._Thompson_Center "James R. Thompson Center").[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-86) This new rail service proposal under active consideration by CTA is currently undergoing Alternatives Analysis Studies.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-87) These studies are the first step in a five-step process. This process is required by the Federal New Starts program,[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-88) which is an essential source of funding for CTA's expansion projects. CTA uses a series of "Screens" to develop a "Locally Preferred Alternative", which is submitted to the federal New Starts program. An [extension of the Red Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Ahead "Red Ahead") was first proposed by then Mayor [Richard J. Daley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_J._Daley "Richard J. Daley") in 1969.[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-89) It would provide service from the current terminus at 95th/Dan Ryan to 130th Street, decreasing transit times for Far South Side residents and relieving crowding and congestion at the current terminus, The CTA presented its locally preferred alternative at meetings in August 2009.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-90) This consists of a new elevated rail line between 95th/Dan Ryan and a new terminal station at 130th Street, paralleling the [Union Pacific Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Pacific_Railroad "Union Pacific Railroad") and the [South Shore Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Shore_Line "South Shore Line"), through the Far South Side neighborhoods of [Roseland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roseland,_Chicago "Roseland, Chicago"), [Washington Heights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Heights,_Chicago "Washington Heights, Chicago"), [West Pullman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Pullman,_Chicago "West Pullman, Chicago"), and [Riverdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riverdale,_Chicago "Riverdale, Chicago").[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-auto2-91) In addition to the terminal station at 130th, three new stations would be built at 103rd, 111th, and Michigan. 2024.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22#cite_note-:6-101) In January 2025, the CTA signed a full funding grant agreement for the
